Disaggregated prefill-decode architectures physically separate the KV cache computation (prefill) from autoregressive generation (decode), routing them to different hardware pools — and prefix sharing exploits the fact that many requests share a common prompt prefix (system prompt, few-shot examples, RAG preamble) so that KV blocks for that prefix can be computed once and reused. The central question is: when a shared prefix is invalidated — because the prompt template changes, a RAG chunk is updated, or a versioned system prompt is rotated — how do you propagate that invalidation across a distributed KV cache without either serving stale activations or destroying the hit rate that made prefix sharing valuable in the first place? A beginner assumes invalidation is a cache eviction problem, analogous to a CDN TTL expiry, but an expert recognizes that the KV cache is activation-space state: a stale block doesn't produce a cache miss error, it silently produces wrong attention over subsequent tokens, making correctness failures invisible at the infrastructure layer. The harder problem is that in disaggregated systems, prefill workers may have already shipped KV blocks to decode workers' local DRAM or HBM before the invalidation signal arrives, creating a window where decode is operating on evicted-but-not-yet-replaced activations with no error signal. Experts also worry about the interaction between prefix tree structure (radix-tree-style block addressing keyed on token IDs) and prompt composition dynamics: if the shared prefix is constructed at request time by concatenating versioned components, a single component version bump invalidates all downstream radix tree nodes, causing a cascading eviction that momentarily collapses hit rate to zero across an entire request class simultaneously — a correlated spike rather than graceful degradation.

In systems like vLLM's prefix caching and SGLang's RadixAttention, prefix equality is defined as bitwise identity of the token ID sequence, meaning two requests share a cache-eligible prefix if and only if their token IDs match exactly up to some block boundary (typically 16 or 32 tokens per block). This is a purely syntactic criterion: a timestamp injected as "2026-06-20" vs "2026-06-19" produces completely different token IDs despite identical semantic structure, so the radix tree treats them as entirely distinct paths with zero shared nodes below the point of divergence. The practical consequence is that any dynamic slot — user ID, session token, retrieved chunk with a freshness timestamp, or even a stochastically sampled few-shot example — acts as a prefix-shattering element: everything before it is potentially shareable, everything at or after it is not, regardless of how much static prompt material follows. SGLang's 2024 paper reports cache hit rates of 80–90% on workloads with stable prefixes (coding assistants, fixed system prompts), but these numbers degrade sharply toward near-zero on per-request dynamic composition without explicit prompt engineering to front-load static content before dynamic slots. The structural assumption being violated is that prompt template similarity implies token sequence similarity — it does not, because the tokenizer operates on the rendered string, and even small lexical changes in early slots cause cascading hash mismatches across all downstream blocks. Sophisticated deployments work around this by canonicalizing dynamic content — moving timestamps to the suffix, hashing retrieved chunks to stable placeholder tokens, or using slot-aware prompt compilers (as in Microsoft's PromptCache work) that pre-tokenize static segments separately — but this requires the application layer to be aware of cache block boundaries, which most LLM application frameworks are not.

The most principled signal available without recomputation is the cross-attention entropy between suffix query vectors and cached prefix key vectors — if the suffix queries concentrate attention sharply on a small subset of prefix positions (low entropy), the cached KV blocks are being used selectively and the frozen representations are likely adequate; if attention is diffuse or if the top-attended prefix positions are semantically misaligned with the suffix topic, degradation is probable. This requires access to the first-layer attention logits between suffix tokens and prefix KV blocks, which are computed anyway during decode prefill of the suffix — so the detector can operate as a lightweight attention pattern classifier on the first forward pass of the suffix without any additional model calls, adding roughly O(suffix_len × prefix_len) operations already subsumed in the attention computation. Concretely, Xiao et al.'s StreamingLLM work and the subsequent "Attention Sink" literature established that certain prefix positions (position 0, early tokens) receive disproportionate attention regardless of content — a detector must control for this structural bias or it will misclassify sink-driven attention concentration as semantic alignment. A complementary signal is suffix query vector distance from the prefix key manifold: if the suffix queries lie far from the subspace spanned by prefix keys in a given layer's head, the suffix is asking questions the prefix was never positioned to answer, which can be computed as a low-rank projection distance without full attention materialization. Pragma-level metadata also helps: if the suffix contains entity tokens (named entities, dates, domain-specific terms) that do not appear or co-occur in the prefix vocabulary, a lightweight token-overlap heuristic — essentially an inverted-index lookup against prefix token IDs — flags high-risk pairs in microseconds, as exploited in approximate retrieval systems like FAISS-based KV indexing proposals from the InfiniGen (2024) paper. The fundamental limitation is that any such detector is operating on surface signals proxying for a semantic judgment — it can identify structural misalignment but cannot rule out that the model's attention mechanism successfully resolves the mismatch at deeper layers, meaning the detector's false negative rate is irreducibly tied to model architecture and cannot be calibrated without ground-truth recomputation on a held-out sample.

One non-obvious fact: in disaggregated prefill-decode architectures, prefix block invalidation must be coordinated across two independent memory hierarchies simultaneously — the prefill worker's GPU HBM (where KV blocks are computed) and the decode worker's CPU DRAM or remote memory pool (where blocks are transferred and held for generation) — and these two invalidation events are not atomic, meaning there exists a window where a block is marked invalid on the prefill side but is still being actively read by a decode worker's attention kernel, with no locking mechanism in current systems (including Mooncake and DistServe as described in their 2024 papers) to prevent this race. The practical consequence is that invalidation in disaggregated serving is not a cache coherence problem in the traditional sense (where a single address space can be protected by a coherence protocol) but rather a distributed transaction problem requiring either a two-phase commit across prefill and decode coordinators or acceptance of a staleness window bounded by the decode worker's block lease duration. Mooncake's architecture sidesteps this partially by making KV transfer pull-based (decode workers request blocks) rather than push-based, which means an invalidated block on the prefill side simply won't be served on the next pull — but any in-flight decode using an already-transferred stale block continues uninterrupted, and the system has no mechanism to abort or restart that generation sequence. The staleness window duration is bounded below by the P2P transfer latency (typically 5–20ms over NVLink or InfiniBand in current clusters) and above by the full decode sequence length, meaning a stale block can corrupt an entire multi-hundred-token generation before the invalidation signal propagates. This implies that TTL-based lease expiry on transferred KV blocks — where decode workers are required to revalidate block freshness against the prefill coordinator after a configurable interval — is the correct primitive, but introduces a revalidation RPC on the critical path of every generation step if the lease is short, creating a latency-throughput tradeoff that no current open-source serving system exposes as a tunable parameter.

response:
LLM inference has an unusual correctness structure that makes strict consistency — no stale blocks ever used — neither necessary nor enforceable at the serving layer: unlike a database transaction where a stale read produces a verifiably wrong answer, a stale KV block produces a subtly shifted probability distribution over next tokens, and there is no ground-truth signal available at inference time to detect this shift without recomputation. What is actually necessary for correctness is a weaker property closer to generation-level atomicity: all KV blocks used within a single forward pass must be mutually consistent with respect to the same prompt version, because mixing blocks from different prompt versions within one attention computation produces incoherent cross-block attention patterns that are strictly worse than using a uniformly stale set of blocks. This implies the relevant guarantee is not consistency in the distributed systems sense but intra-request version isolation — a property analogous to snapshot isolation in databases, where each request sees a coherent point-in-time view of the block store even if that view is not the most recent one. Coherence (eventual replacement) is sufficient for most production workloads because prompt versions change slowly relative to request duration: if a system prompt rotates every few minutes and median generation latency is 2–5 seconds, the fraction of requests that span a version boundary is small, and those requests completing on the old version produce outputs indistinguishable in quality from pre-rotation outputs for most tasks. The dangerous regime is high-frequency dynamic composition — RAG systems where retrieved chunks update per-request, or multi-agent pipelines where the system prompt is modified between turns — where coherence guarantees collapse to near-uselessness because "eventual" replacement arrives after the request has already completed, and the only meaningful guarantee is per-request block version pinning at dispatch time, which Mooncake and vLLM's prefix caching do not implement as an explicit contract.
